cases.interviewerQuestion: When you first hit those stale-state and re-render bugs, what made you realize the problem was architectural—one undifferentiated store—rather than just a bug to patch, and what was the tipping point that pushed you to split things into three layers?
cases.tonyRaw: The pattern I kept seeing was one piece of state - say a document field - triggering re-renders or going stale in places that had no logical reason to care about it, and patching each instance individually just moved the bug rather than fixing it. That told me the real issue was that collaborative state (Liveblocks), server-persisted state (TanStack Query), and local UI state were all living in the same undifferentiated store, so any update anywhere fanned out everywhere. The tipping point was realizing those three have fundamentally different consistency and invalidation models - real-time sync, cache staleness, and ephemeral UI - so I split them into three explicit layers instead of trying to patch one store to behave like three.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Since Chrome extensions can't share cookies with your main app's domain, walk me through how you designed the bearer-token auth flow — where do the tokens get minted, and how do you handle revocation or expiry on the extension side?
cases.tonyRaw: I solo-owned this surface, so I made the call to mint tokens server-side off the main app's existing auth session — the extension would hit an endpoint to exchange that session for a bearer token, which it then stored and attached to every request against the 30+ proxied route handlers. For expiry/revocation, the extension checked token validity on each API call and would kick the user back into a re-auth flow rather than trying to do silent refresh in the background, since the extension context made silent refresh riskier to get right than just prompting re-auth. I'd want to double check the exact TTL we landed on before quoting a number, but the design principle was: keep token lifetime short enough that a stale/revoked token fails fast and visibly, instead of the extension holding onto access longer than the main app would allow.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were integrating AI-generated output into ProseMirror's typed node document model, what specific edge cases or malformed outputs from the model forced you to rethink your state-management design?
cases.tonyRaw: The main issue was that model output came back as loosely-structured text or markdown-ish content that didn't map cleanly onto ProseMirror's strict typed node schema — things like inconsistent nesting or inline formatting that the editor's document model wasn't designed to just absorb. I co-led the team building Mailchimp's first-gen AI content generation feature, and I personally designed the state-management layer to handle this: normalizing and validating AI output before it ever hit the document model, rather than trying to make the schema itself more permissive. cases.interviewerQuestion: Walk me through what actually broke when a meeting transcript exceeded the context window — was it the model silently dropping content, quality degrading, or something else — and how did that failure mode shape your chunking strategy?
cases.tonyRaw: I contributed to Smith rather than architecting it from scratch — the piece I owned was the transcript-chunking and context-window handling. What actually broke on long meetings wasn't a clean truncation error, it was quality degradation: once you got close to the context limit, the model would still respond but start losing track of earlier speakers and decisions, giving confidently wrong summaries instead of failing loudly. That's what shaped the approach — I couldn't rely on the model to tell me when it was struggling, so the chunking logic had to proactively segment transcripts before we hit that degradation zone rather than reacting to errors after the fact.
